slides.title: Two Goals That Disagree
slides.subtitle: no single best answer
slides.paragraphs:
A cheaper design is usually a weaker one. When two goals pull in opposite directions, one solution cannot be best at both.

Multiobjective optimisation keeps the whole set of fair compromises instead of forcing one weighted score.

slides.title: Dominance
slides.subtitle: the only comparison NSGA-II needs

equations.latex: x \prec y \Longleftrightarrow f_m(x) \leq f_m(y)\ \forall m \ \text{and}\ f_k(x) < f_k(y)\ \text{for some}\ k
equations.caption: x dominates y when it is no worse everywhere and better somewhere (all goals minimised)

slides.paragraph: Solutions that nothing dominates form the Pareto front.

slides.title: One Generation
slides.subtitle: parents and children compete together
items: Make children with crossover and mutation.
Merge parents and children into one pool.
Sort the pool into fronts by dominance.
Fill the next population front by front.
Break the tie in the last front by crowding distance.

slides.title: Three Ingredients
slides.subtitle: what makes it NSGA-II

panels.label: Non-dominated sorting
panels.body: Rank every solution by the front it belongs to. Front one is the best.

panels.label: Crowding distance
panels.body: Prefer solutions in sparse regions so the front stays spread out.

panels.label: Elitism
panels.body: Parents compete with children, so a good solution is never lost.

slides.caption: Reference: Deb, Pratap, Agarwal and Meyarivan (2002), IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation 6(2).

slides.title: Crowding Distance
slides.subtitle: how isolated is a solution

equations.caption: neighbours are taken after sorting the front by goal m; the two ends get infinite distance

slides.paragraph: A larger value means fewer neighbours nearby, so the solution is kept.

slides.subtitle: sorting dominates the work
slides.caption: invented values, evaluation cost depends on the problem
slides.paragraph: Non-dominated sorting costs on the order of M times N squared comparisons per generation (Deb et al., 2002).
